screens.title: Amazon EBS: Persistent Block Storage for EC2
screens.narratorSegment: In this module we focus on Amazon Elastic Block Store, or EBS. EBS gives EC2 instances persistent block devices that behave like an attached hard drive. You will learn how EBS differs from ephemeral instance store, why persistence matters for databases and operating systems, and how volume types, snapshots, and encryption fit into common operational workflows. We'll look at practical choices — when to use general purpose gp3 versus provisioned IOPS io2 Block Express, and when to trade cost for throughput with st1 or sc1. You'll also follow a concise lab-style flow: create a gp3 encrypted volume, attach it, format and mount it in Linux, snapshot for backup, and restore from that snapshot. That hands-on flow will anchor the conceptual ideas and highlight common mistakes, like failing to unmount before detaching or forgetting snapshot lifecycle management. By the end of this chapter, you'll be able to select appropriate volume types, manage live volume modifications, and design snapshot and encryption practices that protect data while controlling costs. Consider how these choices affect recovery time and performance for your applications.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Safety
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on the how and the safety practices you must adopt when managing EBS in production. You'll practice creating and attaching a gp3 encrypted volume in the same Availability Zone as your EC2 instance, formatting and mounting it in Linux, and adding test data. Then you'll create a snapshot and restore a new volume from that snapshot to verify recovery. Beyond lab steps, you'll learn to modify volumes on the fly — changing size, IOPS, or volume type without detaching — and to extend the file system inside the OS after modification. Finally, we will highlight common mistakes and cost controls: always unmount before detach to avoid corruption, delete unused snapshots to save costs, and match volume type to workload to avoid overpaying. These skills help you deliver durable storage, quick recovery, and predictable performance for stateful applications.

screens.title: What is EBS and how it differs from instance store
screens.narratorSegment: EBS stands for Elastic Block Store and it provides persistent block-level storage volumes for EC2 instances. Block storage treats data as fixed-size blocks, similar to a raw hard drive, which an operating system can format with a filesystem and mount. The critical distinction is persistence: EBS volumes persist independently of an EC2 instance's lifetime, while instance store volumes are ephemeral and are lost when the instance stops or terminates. This persistence makes EBS suitable for boot volumes, databases, and any application that requires durable, low-latency access to storage. A concrete example: a relational database uses an EBS volume so that data remains intact if the instance is stopped for maintenance; you can then reattach the same EBS volume to another instance in the same Availability Zone. A common misconception is that EBS is a network filesystem; it is not. EBS is block storage attached to a single EC2 instance at a time (except multi-attach special cases not covered here). Key takeaway: choose EBS when you need a durable disk-like device that the OS manages directly, rather than object storage like S3 which serves different use cases.

keyIdea.text: Persistent block storage that behaves like an attached hard drive, surviving instance stops and terminations.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Definition
EBS: Persistent block storage
Block-level storage that the OS formats and mounts. Data persists independently of instance lifecycle.
Analogy
Think of EBS as a removable hard drive you can attach, detach, and reattach to servers in the same Availability Zone. The data stays on the drive even if the server is replaced.
Example
Use an EBS root volume for the OS so the system can be stopped and restarted without losing system files.
Misconception
EBS is not object storage. It cannot be mounted concurrently by many instances like a network file system.
Key Takeaway

EBS gives durable, disk-like volumes for OS and databases; choose it when you need block-level control and persistence.

Comparison: EBS vs Instance Store
Persistence
EBS persists after instance stop/terminate; instance store does not.
Use cases
EBS: boot volumes, databases; instance store: ephemeral caches and temporary data.
Attachment
EBS volumes attach to instances in the same AZ and generally to one instance at a time.

screens.title: EBS Volume Types and When to Use Each
screens.narratorSegment: EBS offers several volume types optimized for different performance and cost profiles. General Purpose SSD volumes, gp2 and gp3, are versatile choices for boot volumes, development environments, and small to medium databases. Key difference: gp2 scales IOPS with size, while gp3 lets you provision IOPS and throughput independently — up to 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 megabytes per second — so you can tune performance without increasing storage capacity. Provisioned IOPS SSD volumes, io1 and io2 Block Express, are built for input and output-intensive, latency-sensitive databases and transactional workloads. io2 Block Express provides the highest IOPS and throughput in the EBS family — values like 256,000 IOPS and 4,000 megabytes per second are available for very large volumes — and also improves durability. For large sequential workloads where throughput matters more than IOPS, choose Throughput Optimized HDD st1, which is cost-effective for big data or log processing. For rarely accessed, cold data, sc1 is the lowest-cost HDD option. A common mistake is selecting st1 for small random input and output workloads; that will cause poor performance. The takeaway: match volume type to access pattern and cost constraints, then monitor and adjust.

keyIdea.title: Volume selection
keyIdea.text: Select volumes by access pattern: gp3 for balanced SSD, io2 Block Express for extreme IOPS, st1/sc1 for throughput/cold data.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Volume Types
Volume types at a glance
Choose based on IOPS, throughput, cost, and access pattern.
gp2 / gp3 — General Purpose SSD
gp3 lets you provision up to 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 MB/s throughput independently of size. Use for boot volumes and general databases.
io1 / io2 Block Express — Provisioned IOPS SSD
Designed for I/O-intensive, transactional systems. io2 Block Express supports very high IOPS and throughput for mission-critical workloads.
st1 — Throughput Optimized HDD
Best for large, sequential I/O like data warehouses and log processing where throughput matters.
sc1 — Cold HDD
Lowest-cost option for infrequently accessed data and cold storage.
Decision guidance
Use these quick checks when choosing a volume type.
If you need consistent, high IOPS
Prefer io2 Block Express for mission-critical DBs that demand low latency and sustained IOPS.
If you need configurable IOPS without increasing size
Choose gp3 to provision IOPS and throughput independently of storage capacity.
If throughput over cost matters
st1 provides cost-effective sequential throughput for analytics and logs.
Key Takeaway

Match volume type to access pattern and cost goal; avoid using HDD types for random I/O databases.

screens.title: Create, Attach, and Detach an EBS Volume
screens.narratorSegment: Creating and attaching an EBS volume is a multistep process that must respect Availability Zone boundaries and operating system state. Start by creating a volume in the same Availability Zone as your target EC2 instance. The AWS CLI example shows the minimal create call for a gp3 volume with encryption enabled. After creation, attach the volume to a running instance with an attach command. Inside the instance, confirm the new block device with a device listing command such as lsblk. Then format and mount the device — for Linux, a common sequence is to create an XFS or ext4 filesystem, create a mount point, and mount the device. Remember: always unmount the filesystem before detaching to avoid corruption. A concrete CLI sequence is shown in the visual; it demonstrates creating, attaching, formatting, verifying with df, and writing a small test file. A common mistake is attempting to attach a volume across Availability Zones — the operation will fail — or detaching without unmounting. Key takeaway: follow the AZ constraint, verify the OS sees the device, and unmount before detach to protect data integrity.

keyIdea.title: Safe attach flow
keyIdea.text: Create volume in same AZ, attach, format, mount, and always unmount before detach to prevent corruption.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Attach / Detach
Step-by-step: create & attach
CLI examples and Linux commands to verify and mount.
$ aws ec2 create-volume --volume-type gp3 --size 10 --availability-zone us-east-1a --encrypted
CreatedVolumeId: vol-0abcdef1234567890

$ aws ec2 attach-volume --volume-id vol-0abcdef1234567890 --instance-id i-0abcdef1234567890 --device /dev/sdf

# On the EC2 instance
$ lsblk
$ sudo mkfs -t xfs /dev/xvdf
$ sudo mkdir /data
$ sudo mount /dev/xvdf /data
$ df -h /data
$ sudo sh -c 'echo "Hello Cohortia" > /data/testfile.txt'
Verification
Use lsblk and df to confirm the device and mounted filesystem before writing data.
Common mistake
Detaching without unmounting risks data corruption. Always unmount first.
Practical tips
  • Volumes can be attached only to instances in the same Availability Zone.
  • A single EBS volume attaches to one instance at a time in most cases — plan for multi-attach only where supported.
  • Use tags to track purpose and ownership of volumes and snapshots to avoid orphaned costs.
Key Takeaway

Follow AZ constraints, verify devices inside the OS, and unmount before detach for safe operations.

screens.title: EBS Snapshots: Incremental Backups and Use Cases
screens.narratorSegment: EBS snapshots are incremental backups of a volume stored in Amazon S3. When you create a snapshot, only the blocks that have changed since the last snapshot are saved, making snapshots storage-efficient. Snapshots are useful for backup and recovery by providing recovery points, and you can copy snapshots across Regions to support disaster recovery. For migration and reproducible images, snapshots can be used to create an AMI or a new volume; creating a new volume from a snapshot lets you resize or change the volume type while preserving data. A typical workflow: snapshot a live volume (preferably after application-level quiescing), then create a new volume from that snapshot in the same or another AZ or Region. A common operational mistake is not deleting old or unneeded snapshots, which accumulate storage costs; implement a lifecycle policy to prune snapshots. Keep in mind snapshots are incremental but the first snapshot copies all used blocks, so schedule accordingly. The practical result: snapshots provide efficient, flexible recovery and migration mechanisms when managed with a clear lifecycle. EBS Snapshots: Incremental Backups and Use Cases means incremental snapshots stored in s3 enable backup, recovery, cross-region disaster recovery, and volume restoration.. In practical terms, how snapshots work and how to use them for backup, disaster recovery, and migration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Snapshots
How snapshots work
Snapshots capture changed blocks and store them in S3 incrementally.
CLI example
$ aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id vol-0abcdef1234567890 --description "Daily backup"
SnapshotId: snap-0abcdef1234567890

# To create a volume from snapshot
$ aws ec2 create-volume --snapshot-id snap-0abcdef1234567890 --availability-zone us-east-1a --volume-type gp3 --size 20
Use cases
Backups, cross-region disaster recovery, AMI creation, and resizing or changing type via restore.
Cost pitfall
Not deleting old snapshots leads to storage costs. Implement lifecycle rules to prune snapshots you no longer need.
Practical guidance
  • First snapshot captures all used blocks; subsequent snapshots are incremental.
  • Prefer application-level quiesce or a consistent checkpoint before snapshotting databases when possible.
  • Use cross-region snapshot copy for disaster recovery and test restores regularly.
Key Takeaway

Snapshots are efficient incremental backups that support recovery and migration, but require lifecycle policies to control cost.

screens.title: EBS Encryption and Key Management
screens.narratorSegment: EBS encryption secures data at rest on volumes and their snapshots by using AWS Key Management Service for encryption keys. When you enable encryption on a volume, all data written to that volume is encrypted, snapshots created from that volume are encrypted, and any new volumes created from such snapshots remain encrypted. By default, AWS supplies a managed KMS key, but for stronger control and compliance you should use customer-managed keys (CMKs). CMKs let you define key rotation policies, granular IAM key usage permissions, and detailed audit trails. A concrete example: creating a gp3 volume with the encrypted flag and a KMS key identifier ensures the data is encrypted from creation. Misconceptions to avoid include believing encryption affects performance dramatically — when managed properly, encryption is largely transparent, and AWS handles cryptographic operations. However, key management policies and access controls must be correct; losing CMK access can make data unrecoverable. The core takeaway: enable encryption for sensitive data and prefer CMKs when you need ownership, compliance reporting, or separate administrative control over keys. EBS Encryption and Key Management means enable ebs encryption to protect data at rest; use customer-managed kms keys for stronger ownership and compliance.. In practical terms, how encryption protects data at rest and why to use customer-managed keys. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Encryption
EBS encryption basics
Encryption covers volumes and snapshots and integrates with AWS KMS.
$ aws ec2 create-volume --volume-type gp3 --size 100 --availability-zone us-east-1a --encrypted --kms-key-id arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456789012:key/your-cmk-id
When to use CMKs
Use customer-managed keys when you need rotation control, audited key access, or strict separation of duties.
Effect on snapshots
Snapshots of encrypted volumes remain encrypted, and new volumes created from encrypted snapshots are encrypted as well.
Operational cautions
  • Ensure correct KMS policies; losing access to a CMK can prevent decryption of volumes and snapshots.
  • Use IAM controls to limit who can create or use CMKs for EBS volumes.
  • Rotate keys and monitor usage for compliance reporting.
Key Takeaway

Encryption is essential for sensitive data; prefer customer-managed keys for control and compliance, but manage key policies carefully.

screens.title: Modify Volumes on the Fly and Extend Filesystems
screens.narratorSegment: EBS supports online modifications, enabling you to change volume size, type, and IOPS for supported types without detaching the volume. This lets you react to growth or performance needs with minimal disruption. After modifying a volume, you typically need to extend the partition and the filesystem inside the operating system so the instance can use the new space. For example, after increasing the volume size via the AWS console or CLI, verify the block device shows the new size with lsblk, then use growpart or parted to resize the partition and finally run a filesystem tool such as xfs_growfs or resize2fs to expand the filesystem. A concrete example: increase a gp3 volume size and IOPS during an unexpected growth spike; modify the volume, then extend the filesystem so the application sees the additional capacity. A common misconception is that changing the EBS size alone makes space instantly usable in the OS; you must extend the filesystem too. The takeaway: leverage online modifications for elasticity, and always complete the OS-level steps to consume the new capacity safely. Modify Volumes on the Fly and Extend Filesystems means you can modify ebs volumes without detach; remember to extend partitions and filesystems in the os afterward.. In practical terms, change size, type, or iops without detaching and then update the os filesystem. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Modify Volumes
Modify without detach
Change size, volume type, or IOPS and apply OS-level extensions.
# Example: modify volume size via CLI
$ aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0abcdef1234567890 --size 50

# On the instance
$ lsblk
$ sudo growpart /dev/xvdf 1
$ sudo xfs_growfs /data
OS steps
After the modify-volume call, resize the partition and filesystem inside the OS to make the space usable.
Tips & cautions
  • Not all volume type changes are instant; check state until modification completes.
  • Test filesystem grow commands in a staging environment before production changes.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Managing EBS in production requires attention to common operational mistakes and an adoption of best practices to avoid them. The top errors include detaching volumes without unmounting from the operating system, which can corrupt data; not deleting obsolete snapshots, which leads to unnecessary storage costs; and selecting the wrong volume type for the workload, such as using st1 for random input and output databases. Best practices include tagging volumes and snapshots to track ownership and purpose, scheduling snapshot lifecycles to remove old backups, and using CMKs for sensitive data where compliance requires explicit key control. Another useful practice is testing snapshot restores periodically to ensure recovery procedures work as expected. A concrete example: an operations team scheduled nightly snapshots but did not delete month-old snapshots, increasing storage costs; implementing a lifecycle policy to retain only the last 30 days solved the cost problem while preserving recovery points. The takeaway: combine safe attach/detach procedures, consistent tagging and lifecycle policies, and the correct volume type selection to minimize downtime and cost. fullNarratorScript:
In this module we focus on Amazon Elastic Block Store, or EBS. EBS gives EC2 instances persistent block devices that behave like an attached hard drive. You will learn how EBS differs from ephemeral instance store, why persistence matters for databases and operating systems, and how volume types, snapshots, and encryption fit into common operational workflows. We'll look at practical choices — when to use general purpose gp3 versus provisioned IOPS io2 Block Express, and when to trade cost for throughput with st1 or sc1. You'll also follow a concise lab-style flow: create a gp3 encrypted volume, attach it, format and mount it in Linux, snapshot for backup, and restore from that snapshot. That hands-on flow will anchor the conceptual ideas and highlight common mistakes, like failing to unmount before detaching or forgetting snapshot lifecycle management. By the end of this chapter, you'll be able to select appropriate volume types, manage live volume modifications, and design snapshot and encryption practices that protect data while controlling costs. Consider how these choices affect recovery time and performance for your applications.

By the end of this chapter you will differentiate EBS volume types and select the right type for real EC2 workloads, perform key volume operations such as creating, attaching, detaching, and modifying volumes, and apply snapshot workflows for backup, disaster recovery, and migration. You will also understand how EBS encryption works with AWS Key Management Service and how to use customer-managed keys for compliance. Each objective connects a measurable action with why it matters: volume selection balances cost and performance, attach/detach discipline prevents corruption, snapshots enable efficient backups and cross-region recovery, and encryption protects data at rest. You'll practice a concise hands-on flow that recreates a production pattern: provision a gp3 encrypted volume in the same Availability Zone as an instance, attach and mount it, take a snapshot, and restore a new volume from that snapshot. This combination of conceptual understanding and practice prepares you to manage persistent storage reliably in AWS while avoiding common mistakes that increase downtime or cost.

These objectives focus on the how and the safety practices you must adopt when managing EBS in production. You'll practice creating and attaching a gp3 encrypted volume in the same Availability Zone as your EC2 instance, formatting and mounting it in Linux, and adding test data. Then you'll create a snapshot and restore a new volume from that snapshot to verify recovery. Beyond lab steps, you'll learn to modify volumes on the fly — changing size, IOPS, or volume type without detaching — and to extend the file system inside the OS after modification. Finally, we will highlight common mistakes and cost controls: always unmount before detach to avoid corruption, delete unused snapshots to save costs, and match volume type to workload to avoid overpaying. These skills help you deliver durable storage, quick recovery, and predictable performance for stateful applications.

EBS stands for Elastic Block Store and it provides persistent block-level storage volumes for EC2 instances. Block storage treats data as fixed-size blocks, similar to a raw hard drive, which an operating system can format with a filesystem and mount. The critical distinction is persistence: EBS volumes persist independently of an EC2 instance's lifetime, while instance store volumes are ephemeral and are lost when the instance stops or terminates. This persistence makes EBS suitable for boot volumes, databases, and any application that requires durable, low-latency access to storage. A concrete example: a relational database uses an EBS volume so that data remains intact if the instance is stopped for maintenance; you can then reattach the same EBS volume to another instance in the same Availability Zone. A common misconception is that EBS is a network filesystem; it is not. EBS is block storage attached to a single EC2 instance at a time (except multi-attach special cases not covered here). Key takeaway: choose EBS when you need a durable disk-like device that the OS manages directly, rather than object storage like S3 which serves different use cases.

EBS offers several volume types optimized for different performance and cost profiles. General Purpose SSD volumes, gp2 and gp3, are versatile choices for boot volumes, development environments, and small to medium databases. Key difference: gp2 scales IOPS with size, while gp3 lets you provision IOPS and throughput independently — up to 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 megabytes per second — so you can tune performance without increasing storage capacity. Provisioned IOPS SSD volumes, io1 and io2 Block Express, are built for input and output-intensive, latency-sensitive databases and transactional workloads. io2 Block Express provides the highest IOPS and throughput in the EBS family — values like 256,000 IOPS and 4,000 megabytes per second are available for very large volumes — and also improves durability. For large sequential workloads where throughput matters more than IOPS, choose Throughput Optimized HDD st1, which is cost-effective for big data or log processing. For rarely accessed, cold data, sc1 is the lowest-cost HDD option. A common mistake is selecting st1 for small random input and output workloads; that will cause poor performance. The takeaway: match volume type to access pattern and cost constraints, then monitor and adjust.

Creating and attaching an EBS volume is a multistep process that must respect Availability Zone boundaries and operating system state. Start by creating a volume in the same Availability Zone as your target EC2 instance. The AWS CLI example shows the minimal create call for a gp3 volume with encryption enabled. After creation, attach the volume to a running instance with an attach command. Inside the instance, confirm the new block device with a device listing command such as lsblk. Then format and mount the device — for Linux, a common sequence is to create an XFS or ext4 filesystem, create a mount point, and mount the device. Remember: always unmount the filesystem before detaching to avoid corruption. A concrete CLI sequence is shown in the visual; it demonstrates creating, attaching, formatting, verifying with df, and writing a small test file. A common mistake is attempting to attach a volume across Availability Zones — the operation will fail — or detaching without unmounting. Key takeaway: follow the AZ constraint, verify the OS sees the device, and unmount before detach to protect data integrity.

EBS snapshots are incremental backups of a volume stored in Amazon S3. When you create a snapshot, only the blocks that have changed since the last snapshot are saved, making snapshots storage-efficient. Snapshots are useful for backup and recovery by providing recovery points, and you can copy snapshots across Regions to support disaster recovery. For migration and reproducible images, snapshots can be used to create an AMI or a new volume; creating a new volume from a snapshot lets you resize or change the volume type while preserving data. A typical workflow: snapshot a live volume (preferably after application-level quiescing), then create a new volume from that snapshot in the same or another AZ or Region. A common operational mistake is not deleting old or unneeded snapshots, which accumulate storage costs; implement a lifecycle policy to prune snapshots. Keep in mind snapshots are incremental but the first snapshot copies all used blocks, so schedule accordingly. The practical result: snapshots provide efficient, flexible recovery and migration mechanisms when managed with a clear lifecycle. EBS Snapshots: Incremental Backups and Use Cases means incremental snapshots stored in s3 enable backup, recovery, cross-region disaster recovery, and volume restoration.. In practical terms, how snapshots work and how to use them for backup, disaster recovery, and migration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

EBS encryption secures data at rest on volumes and their snapshots by using AWS Key Management Service for encryption keys. When you enable encryption on a volume, all data written to that volume is encrypted, snapshots created from that volume are encrypted, and any new volumes created from such snapshots remain encrypted. By default, AWS supplies a managed KMS key, but for stronger control and compliance you should use customer-managed keys (CMKs). CMKs let you define key rotation policies, granular IAM key usage permissions, and detailed audit trails. A concrete example: creating a gp3 volume with the encrypted flag and a KMS key identifier ensures the data is encrypted from creation. Misconceptions to avoid include believing encryption affects performance dramatically — when managed properly, encryption is largely transparent, and AWS handles cryptographic operations. However, key management policies and access controls must be correct; losing CMK access can make data unrecoverable. The core takeaway: enable encryption for sensitive data and prefer CMKs when you need ownership, compliance reporting, or separate administrative control over keys. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

EBS supports online modifications, enabling you to change volume size, type, and IOPS for supported types without detaching the volume. This lets you react to growth or performance needs with minimal disruption. After modifying a volume, you typically need to extend the partition and the filesystem inside the operating system so the instance can use the new space. For example, after increasing the volume size via the AWS console or CLI, verify the block device shows the new size with lsblk, then use growpart or parted to resize the partition and finally run a filesystem tool such as xfs_growfs or resize2fs to expand the filesystem. A concrete example: increase a gp3 volume size and IOPS during an unexpected growth spike; modify the volume, then extend the filesystem so the application sees the additional capacity. A common misconception is that changing the EBS size alone makes space instantly usable in the OS; you must extend the filesystem too. The takeaway: leverage online modifications for elasticity, and always complete the OS-level steps to consume the new capacity safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A common slip is assuming device naming is identical across instance types; always confirm the device seen by the OS. Ready your terminal and follow the exact commands shown in the visual area.

Managing EBS in production requires attention to common operational mistakes and an adoption of best practices to avoid them. The top errors include detaching volumes without unmounting from the operating system, which can corrupt data; not deleting obsolete snapshots, which leads to unnecessary storage costs; and selecting the wrong volume type for the workload, such as using st1 for random input and output databases. Best practices include tagging volumes and snapshots to track ownership and purpose, scheduling snapshot lifecycles to remove old backups, and using CMKs for sensitive data where compliance requires explicit key control. Another useful practice is testing snapshot restores periodically to ensure recovery procedures work as expected. Let's apply what you've learned with two practical assessment scenarios. First scenario: a high-transaction financial database expects sustained millions of transactions per second and must have the highest durability and consistent low-latency input and output. The correct EBS choice for this workload is a provisioned IOPS SSD like io2 Block Express because it offers the highest IOPS, throughput, and durability in the EBS family. The contrast is using a general purpose volume, which would not guarantee the sustained performance needed. Second scenario: a developer accidentally deletes files on a live EBS volume but daily snapshots exist. The most efficient recovery is to create a new volume from the latest good snapshot, attach it to the running instance as a secondary volume, and copy the needed files back. This approach avoids significant downtime and does not require replacing the active root volume. Let's summarize the core concepts. First: EBS is persistent block storage for EC2 suitable for boot volumes, databases, and stateful workloads. Second: choose volume types by matching access patterns — gp3 for general SSD workloads with configurable IOPS, io2 Block Express for extreme IOPS and throughput, st1 for sequential throughput, and sc1 for cold data. Third: snapshots are incremental backups stored in S3 used for recovery, migration, and AMI creation; manage snapshot lifecycle to control cost. Fourth: encryption with KMS secures data at rest; use customer-managed keys when you need stronger control and auditable policies. Fifth: follow safe operations — create volumes in the same Availability Zone, verify devices inside the OS, unmount before detach, and extend filesystems after online modification. These concepts combined help you design storage that balances performance, durability, security, and cost. As you practice in the lab, reflect on how each decision affects recovery time and operational complexity.

Keep these three reminders front of mind as you design storage for EC2. First, always match the EBS volume type to the workload: SSD for random input and output, provisioned IOPS for mission-critical DBs, and HDD for throughput-focused workloads. Second, use snapshots for efficient backups and cross-region recovery, but apply lifecycle policies to avoid accumulating cost. Third, enable EBS encryption for sensitive data and prefer customer-managed KMS keys when you need key control and compliance reporting. When you combine correct selection, snapshot discipline, and encryption practices, you achieve a balance of performance, durability, security, and cost control. Before finishing a design or running a lab, run a quick checklist: is the volume in the right AZ, is encryption configured, are snapshots being retained by a policy, and have you planned for safe attach/detach procedures?
